rule.test: either player's account played >= min_games in the window AND used exactly one distinct team
rule.tempo_clause: ADDED 2026-09-30 (MEASURE, abra/regmc 1.36.0). An account with a game whose id matches tempo_applies_id_pattern (Reg M-C and later) is flagged only if it ALSO played >= min_games_in_one_day games on one calendar day. On Reg M-C the 50-game / one-team test flagged 15 bo1 and 8 bo3 accounts. Seven of them form a separate cluster, 120-600 games in one day: Thornlace48812, kevdan42, Scorecard-Pokemon, SC-SME, SC-Control, AI_Paku, Crituvyn72957. None forfeited more than 0.6% of their games, and all are absent from the live top 500. The other 16 (monfish counted once per store) sit at 12-48 games on their busiest day. Eleven of them lost 1-33% of their games by forfeit, which is a human act. Two hold live top-500 ranks: Novicebest, bo1 #290, and Afmoad, bo3 #109, both fetched 2026-09-30 01:33Z. The gap between the clusters is 48 to 120 games in one day, and the cut sits inside it. On a Reg M-B corpus no id matches the pattern, so Reg M-B's bot set is unchanged. docs/_reports/2026-09-30-regmc-store-quality.md
rule.rationale: Name-based detection only catches accounts that announce themselves. These five did not, and they appeared in 52.2% of the games the name filter called clean. The decisive signal is team invariance: Carchdraw84172 played 459 games with exactly one team, 367 of them in a single day - a game every four minutes for twenty-four hours without changing a slot. Active human accounts (15-60 games) reuse their most-common team about 64% of the time, never 100%.

caught: HospitalityCheck (55, 1) - crossed the threshold on 2026-07-25 as the store grew to 8,356. Unlike the other five its name is NOT machine-shaped, so the corroborating evidence below does not extend to it.
evidence.false_positive_check: No account with >=50 games in this store has more than one distinct team, so the rule separates cleanly. It is stable for thresholds between 50 and 100 games.
evidence.corroborating: The original five share a machine-shaped name (Word+5 digits), forfeit 16-23% of games against a human median of 42%, and run the same two-day burst pattern. HospitalityCheck matches the team-invariance rule (55 games, 1 team) but not the naming pattern, and sits just above the 50-game threshold - it is the weakest of the six and the one to re-examine first if the rule is ever loosened.

rule.known_limitation: Threshold-based, so a bot playing under 50 games or varying its team escapes. This raises the floor on bot detection; it does not establish one. The remaining set must still be described as 'no bot detected', never as 'human'.
